subject: Banking
title: Managing Employment
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Managing Employment.

hook.text: The Fed has a dual mandate: stable prices and maximum employment. Most central banks only target inflation.

buildup.text: When unemployment rises, the Fed cuts rates to stimulate borrowing, spending, and hiring. Cheap money creates jobs.

discovery.text: There's a tension: low unemployment can cause inflation, and fighting inflation can cause unemployment.

twist.text: The Phillips Curve looked stable until stagflation proved unemployment and inflation can rise together.

climax.text: Central banks influence employment through interest rates, but they can't create jobs directly.

punchline.text: Stable prices and full employment. The Fed's impossible balancing act.

quiz.question: What is the Fed's dual mandate?

details.summary: The Federal Reserve has a dual mandate to pursue both price stability and maximum employment. Balancing these goals requires careful judgment because policies that fight inflation often increase unemployment and vice versa.
details.whyItMatters: Central bank employment policy affects whether millions of people have jobs. The trade-off between fighting inflation and preserving employment is one of the most consequential decisions in economic policy.
takeaways: The dual mandate is unique to the Fed among major central banks
The Phillips curve theorizes an inverse relationship between inflation and unemployment
The natural rate of unemployment is a key concept but difficult to measure

faq.question: What is the Fed's dual mandate?
faq.answer: Congress requires the Fed to pursue both maximum employment and stable prices. Unlike the European Central Bank, which focuses primarily on inflation, the Fed must balance both goals even when they conflict.

faq.question: How does raising interest rates affect employment?
faq.answer: Higher rates make borrowing more expensive for businesses, slowing expansion and hiring. If rates rise too fast, businesses cut jobs and unemployment rises. The Fed tries to find the rate that controls inflation with minimum job losses.
